name: The Painters' School
firstVisit: Dust, and the smell of old linseed. Nobody's been in here for a very long time.
The paintings have come down off the far wall. All of them.

1: The door back out to the South Road. The boards you pulled off are lying in the grass.
V: Plaster, flaking. Someone's tested colours on it in little squares: twelve greens, nine blues, one red.
B: A window, boarded over from outside. Daylight comes through the cracks in stripes.
H: Four bare hooks in a row, and under each a clean square on the plaster where a painting hung.
Under the squares, four little brass plates: I. WONDER. II. DUTY. III. DOUBT. IV. PEACE.
e: An easel, and on it a canvas that was never finished: a sky, and a pencil line where the ground should be.
S: A statue of an old man, a brush tucked behind his ear and his sleeves rolled up. His students made it; you can tell. One arm's longer than the other.
The plaque says: OUR MASTER, WHO TAUGHT US TO LOOK.
Somebody's left a paintbrush at his feet. It's been there a long time.
C: The master's stool, facing the wall where the paintings hung. There's paint on the seat. He sat in it anyway.
k: A student's desk. On it, a sketchbook, left open.
Sparrows, mostly. Horses with the legs not quite right. A man in a crown, laughing, the crown on crooked. An old man cleaning a brush, again and again.
Every page is signed in the corner, small: B.
w: A painting, fallen face up in the dust: a field at morning. A sword stands planted in the earth, and a sparrow sits on its hilt.
There's no boy in this one. A corner's still in pencil.
x: A painting, fallen face up in the dust: a boy kneeling on a studio floor in front of an old man with paint on his hands.
A sword lies on the boards between them. Neither of them is looking at it.
y: A painting, fallen face up in the dust: a small boy at a window, drawing the birds outside.
Behind him, in the corner, a sword leans against the wall, much too big for him. He hasn't noticed it.
z: A painting, fallen face up in the dust: the boy, older, holding up a sword with both arms. It's heavier than he is.
A king and a queen watch from a balcony, very pleased.
